title: Bi-national academic funding and collaboration dynamics: the case of the German-Israeli foundation
short_title: Does bi-national funding sustain research collaboration?

affiliations.1: Department of Information Science, Bar Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel
affiliations.4: Knowledge Technologies for the Social Sciences, GESIS–Leibniz-Institute for the Social Sciences, Mannheim, Germany

abstract: Academic grant programs are widely used to motivate international research collaboration and boost scientific impact across borders. Among these, bi-national funding schemes–pairing researchers from just two designated countries–are common yet understudied compared with national and multinational funding. In this study, we explore whether bi-national programs are associated with new collaborations and lasting partnerships. To this end, we conducted an observationa bibliometric case study of the German–Israeli Foundation (GIF), covering 642 grants, 2386 researchers, and 52,847 publications. Our results show that GIF funding is associated with increased co-authorship behavior during, and even slightly before, the grant period, but it is rarely linked with long-lasting co-authorship patterns that persist once the funding concludes. By tracing co-authorship before, during, and after the funding period, clustering collaboration trajectories with temporally ware K-means, and predicting cluster membership with ML models, we find that 45% of teams with no prior co-authored publications become active while funded, yet activity declines rapidly post-award; roughly one-third sustain longer-term co-authorship activity, whereas only a small subset sustains high, lasting co-authorship activity. Moreover, the team’s composition and bibliometrics are found to be largely insufficient in predicting co-authorship activity during and after the grant.
summary: Do international research grants lead to lasting partnerships? We studied 642 German–Israeli Foundation grants involving 2,386 researchers and 52,847 publications. Co-authorship commonly increased around the funding period, but often declined afterward. About 45% of teams with no previous joint publications became active while funded. This observational study describes associations with funding and does not establish that grants caused the changes.
key_findings: 45% of teams with no prior co-authored publications became active during funding.
Co-authorship activity often declined after funding; roughly one-third sustained longer-term activity.
Team composition and bibliometric features were largely insufficient to predict collaboration trajectories.
The observational design identifies associations rather than causal effects of funding.
